name: Brăila
title: Brăila Hull Thickness Measurement | Danube Grain and Cargo Ships
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Brăila for grain carriers, river-sea ships and barges on the Danube: hold, tank and hull gauging for survey and sale.
h1: Ship Gauging and UTM at Brăila on the Danube
intro: Brăila is the farthest inland Romanian port that seagoing ships can reach on the Danube, and it has long been a grain town. Bulk carriers and river-sea ships load cereals, oilseeds and metal products at its quays, and barge convoys pass through constantly. A team mobilised from India can gauge a ship here during a cargo call or a lay-by, giving the superintendent measured figures for a survey, a repair or a purchase.

highlights.h: The last port for seagoing ships
highlights.p: Brăila marks the practical limit of upriver navigation for ocean-going vessels on the Danube. Ships that reach it have made a long passage from the sea, and gauging here is a chance to measure holds and ballast tanks after that run.

Cereals, sunflower seed and rapeseed are loaded here in volume, and grabs, loaders and returning cargo residues wear tank tops and frames. Measurement in the clean empty hold before loading shows where plating has thinned.

Outside the main export months, ships and barges lie at Brăila with space to work. Those periods suit unhurried tank and hold programmes, with entry preparation done properly instead of squeezed between loading shifts.

port.h: Brăila: a grain port at the top of the sea-going Danube
p: Brăila lies on the left bank of the Danube, upstream of Galați, in the flat plain of the Bărăgan that feeds much of Romania's agricultural exports. The river here is wide, and the port occupies a long stretch of the waterfront in the city. For seagoing ships it is effectively the end of the line: beyond Brăila, the river is crossed by fixed bridges and shallower reaches that limit height and draught, and traffic is largely river-sea ships and barges. Seasonal water level controls the loaded draught and therefore how fully ships can load.

The traffic mix follows agriculture. At harvest time, grain moves out in volume to the Mediterranean and beyond, either loaded onto seagoing ships directly or shipped downriver by barge for transhipment at Constanța. Metal products, fertiliser and general cargo also pass the quays, and the port has a long history of ship repair and shipbuilding on the river. A suspension bridge now crosses the Danube near the city, and a vessel's height above water determines whether it can pass beneath, a point that matters for tall ships and floating equipment on the move.

Inspection demand follows the age of the fleet. Many river-sea ships and barges serving Brăila were built decades ago and are now on their third or fourth survey cycle, so their thickness records are long and the remaining margins are narrow. Bulk carriers that come to load grain are often older tonnage working the Black Sea and Mediterranean, with holds that show frame and tank-top wear. Between harvests, owners use quieter weeks for the survey and gauging work that cannot be done under cargo gear, which makes the shoulder seasons the best time to attend.

facilities.h: Where ships can be gauged at Brăila
p: Brăila has long-established river repair facilities, but their capacity and operating status vary, so a superintendent planning a docking or a lift should confirm with the ship's agent what the yards on the river offer for the required dates. For gauging that does not need a dock, the quays are the main working place: after a ship has been discharged and before it loads, empty holds can be measured at frames, tank top, hoppers and bulkheads, and ballast tanks and deck plating can be reached at the same time.

Barges and river-sea ships also lie along the riverbank in fleeting areas and at lay-by berths between voyages. Those quiet positions are well suited to a deliberate programme, with tank ventilation and entry permits organised in advance and the measurement grid worked through methodically. Bottom plating below the waterline cannot be measured from outside on a floating ship, so where an owner wants complete coverage, the sensible sequence is to measure internal structure at Brăila and complete the shell during a docking at Galați, Constanța or another yard.
list: Public cargo quays — grain, oilseeds, metal products and general cargo; empty holds and deck gauged between discharge and loading.
Grain terminal berths — loading points for bulk carriers; hold frames, hoppers and hatch coamings measured in clean holds before cargo.
River repair yards — ship and barge repair on the Danube; scope and capacity to be confirmed before a docking is planned.
Barge fleeting and lay-by berths — convoys and river-sea ships between voyages; tank and shell gauging where access allows.
River anchorage — ships awaiting a berth in the busy season; deck and ballast tank measurement by boat with the agent's help.

context.h: Danube rules, port state control and trade conditions
p: Port state control for seagoing ships at Brăila is exercised by the Romanian Naval Authority under the Paris MoU and the Black Sea MoU. Because many ships here are older, expanded inspection is a real possibility, and structural findings on hatch coamings, deck fittings and ballast tanks are the kind that can lead to a deficiency. If those areas have already been measured, the owner can answer an inspector's questions with figures, and decide on repairs before the ship comes up for inspection instead of after.

Rules from the EU apply as for any Romanian port: the Inventory of Hazardous Materials for ships entering Union ports, emissions trading for qualifying voyages and FuelEU Maritime. On the Danube, there are further practical limits, among them the height under the bridge near the city, water level in the river and winter ice in cold years. Since 2022, Ukrainian cargo has also been moving through the Danube system, which has made the lower river busier and the berths more crowded than in earlier years, but it has not changed how gauging is done.

psc: Paris MoU and Black Sea MoU

jobs.p: Work here tends to follow the grain calendar and the river fleet's survey cycle. An owner who knows a bulk carrier will load at Brăila can have the holds measured before cargo, and an owner of river-sea tonnage can use a lay-by for a full programme. Each scope below is set from the survey status, the access the berth allows and the spaces that are empty on the day, and agreed with the superintendent before the team travels from India.
list: Hold gauging on a grain carrier before loading at Brăila, covering frames, tank top, lower brackets and hatch coamings.
Survey preparation on an older river-sea ship, measuring internal structure and deck plating ahead of a docking elsewhere on the river.
Barge hull measurement for a fleet owner deciding which units to repair and which to retire, focused on shell, bottom and framing.
Ballast tank gauging on a seagoing bulk carrier at the end of a long river passage, to record wastage before the next special survey.
Pre-purchase gauging of a river-sea ship lying at a Brăila berth, giving the buyer deck, hold and tank readings.

logistics: The usual route is Bucharest Henri Coandă Airport followed by a journey of a few hours by road or rail, with Galați reachable on the way for ships at both ports. The quays and yards are controlled facilities, so the ship's agent applies for access for each technician and the instruments from passport details sent in advance. Romania is within Schengen, so the team coming from India needs Schengen visas, and we fix travel dates around the visa decision and the ship's berthing window.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged on a grain ship at Brăila?
faqs.a: Yes, once they are empty and clean. The best moment is after discharge or before the first load goes in, when frames, tank top, hoppers and bulkheads can be reached. Once grain is aboard the holds are closed to us, and only ballast tanks, deck plating and hatch covers can be measured during loading.

faqs.q: Is Brăila a good place for UTM before a docking?
faqs.a: It can be. If a ship will dock elsewhere on the Danube or at the coast, gauging at Brăila beforehand lets the owner see how much steel is likely to be needed and arrange material in advance. The underwater shell still needs the dock itself, but internal structure measured earlier shortens the time in the yard.

faqs.q: Does the Danube water level change how you plan work?
faqs.a: It influences the ship's schedule rather than the measurement. Low water can limit loading and hold ships at the berth, while high water can change the arrival window. We plan around the ship's confirmed dates, ask for notice of any change and adjust the travel and visas for the technicians to match.

faqs.q: Can you gauge barges and push-tow units?
faqs.a: Yes. They need a tighter measurement grid because plating is thin and wear is concentrated in grab-discharge trades. We set the points against the class or inland waterway standard the barge works to and deliver readings in a form the owner and surveyor can use. Where access to bottom plating is not possible afloat, we say so in the report.

faqs.q: Do you cover Galați and Constanța on the same trip?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Galați is a short distance downriver and Constanța is the sea port on the coast. For a fleet with ships at more than one of them, one mobilisation from India with an ordered route saves travel and uses the Schengen visas more fully, provided the berthing dates for each ship line up.
